reader.decision_reason: The message gives a coherent mechanism: a nested pool acquisition deadlocks when the pool is exhausted. Passing the open connection removes the cause, and the only cost it states is a signature change with no other callers found. The config-only alternative just moves the failure point.

reconstruction.problem: `checkout` holds a pooled connection and calls `hold_seats`, which requests a second connection from the same pool. With max_size=10 and 14 requests in flight, 10 requests hold connections while waiting for a second one, and 4 requests wait for a first one. Nobody can proceed.
reconstruction.what_breaks: Checkout freezes until the 30 s pool timeout fires. Then all 14 requests raise PoolTimeout and return 500 at once. The next queued batch repeats this, so the freeze recurs for as long as the burst lasts. Postgres sat at 38 of 200 connections, so the pool cap was the limit, not the database. At normal traffic (about 3 in flight) the pool never empties, so the bug stays hidden. The seat hold also commits on its own connection, so a failure after line 12 can leave seats held for 10 minutes with no order.
reconstruction.fix: Change `hold_seats` to `hold_seats(conn, event_id, seat_ids)` and run `conn.execute` on the connection it receives. Delete the `pool` import from `app/seats.py`. Update the call in `app/checkout.py` to pass `conn`. Each request then needs one connection, and the seat hold joins the order transaction. As a stopgap only, raise `max_size` or lower `timeout`.
reconstruction.cost: The signature of `hold_seats` changes, so any other caller must pass a connection. The message says it found none in this repository. The config alternative only raises the load at which the deadlock appears. At 4 replicas, max_size=10 already uses 40 connections against the limit of 200.

reader.closing_answer: Yes. Apply the `conn` change to `app/seats.py` and `app/checkout.py`.
